title: Don't Resample — Rewind to the Bad Token
hook: Resampling after a failure throws away the reasoning that was still correct. TTEL finds the token where things went wrong and branches from there — same pass@64, half the tokens.
key_points: Independent sampling and multi-turn refinement both lack token-level credit assignment, so valid reasoning prefixes get discarded.
TTEL compares conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline to isolate the step where the error occurred.
It then truncates the trajectory at that point and branches a new generation, reusing the maximal valid prefix.
On LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B it hits pass@64 of 71.0% using 360.4k tokens against 735.0k for independent sampling.
The authors report strictly dominating Pareto frontiers on pass@k versus generated-token cost.
Gains carry over to AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 on both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.
content_html: Spending more compute at inference time reliably improves reasoning and coding performance. The two standard ways of spending it — sample n independent attempts, or refine sequentially over several turns — share a blind spot: neither knows which token went wrong, so a failed attempt is thrown away in its entirety, valid prefix included.
extra_html:
Localize, truncate, branch

Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL) uses fixed or environment feedback to do token-level error localization. The trick is a contrast: run the trajectory's conditional probabilities under the informed feedback and again against a null-context baseline, and the step where the two diverge is the step where the error was introduced. TTEL then truncates the trajectory right there and branches a fresh generation, keeping the maximal valid prefix instead of paying to regenerate it.

What it buys

The authors report strictly dominating Pareto frontiers on pass@k versus generated-token cost across sequential reasoning domains. Concretely, Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench reaches pass@64 of 71.0% while generating roughly half the tokens of independent sampling (360.4k against 735.0k). The result generalizes to the math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 on both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, outperforming competing test-time baselines. The broader lesson is that token-level credit assignment is available at inference time, not just during training. Chitale and colleagues, arXiv 2026.

related.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting
related.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.

related.title: Interaction Scaling: Grounding the Third Axis of Test-Time Compute
related.hook: Reasoning longer and sampling more both mine the same frozen weights — they can't tell a model anything new. Let it poke a real tool instead, and a coding loop hits 100% pass rate with zero variance.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

related.title: The Shadow Price of Reasoning
related.hook: When you can't afford to let every query think as long as it wants, who gets the compute? Treat reasoning tokens like a scarce resource and economics gives a clean answer.

flashcards.prompt: What waste does TTEL target in ordinary best-of-n sampling?
flashcards.back_html: Without token-level credit assignment, a failed trajectory is discarded whole — including the prefix that was perfectly valid up to the point of the actual mistake.

flashcards.prompt: How does TTEL find the token where reasoning went wrong?

choices.text: It compares conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline
It asks a separate critic model to annotate each step as correct or incorrect
It re-runs the trajectory with a higher temperature and looks for divergence

flashcards.explanation_html: The signal comes from how much the feedback shifts token probabilities relative to a no-feedback baseline, which localizes the error without needing per-step labels.

flashcards.prompt: What does 'strictly dominating Pareto frontier' mean in this paper's results?
flashcards.back_html: At any token budget TTEL reaches a higher pass@k than the baselines — e.g. pass@64 of 71.0% on LiveCodeBench with about half the tokens of independent sampling.
